content.p: On the night of 17 June 1992, armed men from the KwaMadala Hostel attacked the Joe Slovo informal settlement in Boipatong, a township near Vereeniging in the Vaal Triangle. Most sources put the number of people killed at 45, among them women and babies. The attackers were supporters of the Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP). The victims were residents of the settlement; the IOL report calls them African National Congress (ANC) supporters.

The killings fell at a delicate moment, while the ANC and the National Party government were negotiating a new constitution at the Convention for a Democratic South Africa, known as Codesa. Within days the ANC had accused the government and the police of complicity and had suspended the talks. Whether the police really played any part has been argued over for more than thirty years. A criminal trial, an inquiry led by a British expert and a Truth and Reconciliation Commission amnesty panel all found no proof of it. The commission's own main report said the opposite.

South African History Online describes a group of about 300 armed men from the KwaMadala Hostel who attacked the settlement. It says the men were affiliated to the IFP and carried machetes and spears. Observers at the time suspected that the assault was meant to undermine the negotiations between the government and the ANC. The FW de Klerk Foundation says the victims were hacked and stabbed to death and calls the massacre egregious even by the violent standards of the period.

The same history site refers to one of the more shocking details attributed to the night: that one attacker drove a spear through a two-year-old child held in his mother's arms. A photograph credited to Greg Marinovich shows women mourning nine-month-old Aaron Mathope, who was killed in the attack.

The death toll varies slightly with the source. The O'Malley Archives, the FW de Klerk Foundation, IOL and a justice department summary of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission material speak of 45 dead, while the Mail & Guardian says more than 40. A University of Cape Town news report on a master's thesis about the massacre says "at least 39" people were killed.
content.h2: A week of visits and anger
content.p: Politicians and church leaders came quickly. On 18 June Joe Slovo and Cyril Ramaphosa of the ANC visited Boipatong, and Ramaphosa accused President F.W. de Klerk and the police of complicity. Archbishop Desmond Tutu visited grieving families on 19 June, followed by Ray Macauley.

De Klerk came on Saturday 20 June, under heavy police guard, to express sympathy. South African History Online says residents were angered rather than comforted and chanted "To hell with de Klerk -- go away." His motorcade drove slowly down Bakoena Street, the road that divides the bungalows of Boipatong from Slovo Park, and stopped. The crowd surged forward and clashed with his security team, and he stayed in his vehicle. After a tense fifteen minutes he left, with people chasing his convoy. According to the same account, armoured vehicles then moved in, one person was shot dead by police, and officers opened fire on a crowd that was trying to identify the body.

On 21 June Nelson Mandela visited with Ramaphosa and other ANC leaders. On the field where police had fired the day before, he said he was "convinced we are no longer dealing with human beings but animals," and that the ANC would not forget what De Klerk, the National Party and the IFP had done. Two days later, on 23 June, the ANC's National Executive Committee suspended negotiations, citing the government's alleged complicity.

The Goldstone Commission, set up to examine political violence during the transition, asked the British criminologist Dr Peter Waddington to investigate. According to South African History Online, he noted that the police had not collected fingerprints, blood samples or other evidence that could have identified the killers and secured convictions. He nonetheless reported that there was no evidence of police complicity or involvement. He concluded that the South African Police lacked proper investigative procedures, even in a case as sensitive as this.

In 1993 members of the IFP were arrested, tried and convicted. South African History Online says about 100 Boipatong residents and five state witnesses testified. Two other publications give different figures: the O'Malley Archives and the FW de Klerk Foundation both refer to 120 residents, and the UCT report says the court acted on the tested evidence of 120. These sources add that not one of the residents who testified, in the words of these sources, saw police vehicles helping the attackers or claimed that white men were present.

The O'Malley Archives, summarising a piece by the writer Rian Malan, adds that five accomplices who testified for the state in return for immunity rejected the charge of police complicity, and called reports of masked white gunmen "infamous lies."
content.h2: The commission and the amnesty committee
content.p: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) took up Boipatong in two different ways, and the two did not agree. In its October 1998 report the commission found that "KwaMadala residents, with the police, planned and carried out" the killings. The FW de Klerk Foundation says the report claimed security forces had ferried the attackers to the township in police vehicles and that white men with blackened faces were among them. A justice department media summary of May 1999 adds that the commission accepted claims that police had ignored warnings of an attack, and that police armoured vehicles known as Casspirs had dropped the killers off. It also records the commission's finding that police destroyed evidence.

Malan challenged the finding. According to the O'Malley Archives, he argued that the commission had carried out no investigation of the massacre itself and had accepted accusations made in the confusion after it, and that a large part of its text was copied word for word from a June 1992 report by an ANC-supporting monitoring group. These are Malan's claims.

Meanwhile, 16 convicted men from the hostel applied for amnesty, together with a 17th applicant, Andries Nosenga, who had not been convicted for Boipatong. The Mail & Guardian reported in October 2000 that all of them, except Nosenga, denied any security force role. Vincent Khanyile told the commission in 1998, according to South African History Online, that the reason was revenge, and he claimed that a week earlier three IFP members had been shot dead by Self Defence Units in Boipatong. Residents of Boipatong opposed amnesty, and some of them also believed the security forces had been involved.

Nosenga was the exception. In January 1999 he submitted a statement that, according to the justice department summary, revived the claims of police collusion and named high-level IFP figures. He said that the gang leader Victor Kheswa, known as the "Vaal Monster," had played a leading role and that Sergeant Pedro Peens of the local murder and robbery squad had masterminded the attack. Peens denied it. Malan reported that Kheswa was in police custody on the night, and the other applicants also denied that Kheswa was there. The applicants' lawyers asked the committee to look into whether Nosenga had been coerced or influenced into applying falsely. They also argued that the commission's earlier finding had prejudged their clients, because applicants who contradicted it risked being judged to have lied.

In October 2000 Piers Pigou, a former TRC investigator, wrote in the Mail & Guardian that the apartheid hitman Ferdi Barnard had told the amnesty committee that, days before the massacre, he was told guns would go to KwaMadala residents, who would attack the ANC. Barnard could not say whether security forces were involved. Pigou also noted that the committee had received a transcript of a conversation in which a security policeman told Malan he had been in the township in an armoured vehicle that night. The original police investigation had not mentioned such a vehicle. The committee decided the policeman's testimony took the matter no further. Pigou concluded that no significant inquiry had ever been held into security force involvement.

The committee ruled in 2000. In November 2000 IOL reported that 13 members of the IFP had been granted amnesty, among them Vincent Khanyile, Timothy Stals and Mhlupeki Tshabangu. A TRC spokesman, Mbulelo Sompetha, said the commission could not independently prove that white people had been present. The O'Malley Archives reports that the committee found the hostel supporters had carried out the killings on their own, without police help, in revenge for repeated attacks by ANC supporters, and that it judged the eyewitness testimony of police involvement untruthful or mistaken. The UCT report says it found the evidence of police complicity "fraught with difficulties."

All of the sources agree that Boipatong altered the course of the transition, but they disagree on how. Malan, as summarised by the O'Malley Archives, argued that the talks had actually stalled a month earlier because of a deadlock the ANC engineered, and that after Boipatong De Klerk went from riding high to being seen as "just another racist." By September 1992, he wrote, the government's negotiators made "extraordinary concessions." The FW de Klerk Foundation likewise says the ANC used the massacre as a pretext to suspend talks and launch rolling mass action. South African History Online takes a different view. It says the massacre may have strengthened the resolve of those who wanted a peaceful settlement, may have heralded the end of Codesa I, and paved the way for Codesa II and the elections less than two years later.

The UCT report quotes James Simpson, whose thesis examined the case, as saying the ANC gained enormous political capital by broadcasting Boipatong as state-sponsored violence while the evidence of complicity was "thin and incoherent." He also argued that popular anger spoke to a broader reality, in which the state had repeatedly tried to undermine the ANC by underhand and often violent means. The report adds that De Klerk began loosening his ties with the IFP.

South African History Online adds that most accounts still explain the attack as the apartheid government's attempt to weaken the ANC through the IFP, but it calls that explanation incomplete. It points to years of everyday contact between hostel residents and township residents, and to the arrival of families displaced from white farms, as factors that need study. The FW de Klerk Foundation records that the EFF said in 2020, on the 28th anniversary, that the massacre was orchestrated by an apartheid government led by De Klerk. De Klerk's foundation sets against that account the findings of the 1993 trial, the Goldstone Commission, Waddington and the amnesty committee. Pigou, writing in 2000, said the question had never been properly examined.
